question: A synthetic adult starting colorectal-cancer chemotherapy has lost 8% of body weight in two months, is eating less than usual, and still has a BMI of 25. What nutrition screening and follow-up assessment are appropriate, and does the normal BMI rule out a nutrition problem?

cards.description: Weight loss, intake, BMI, muscle function, and nutrition assessment
cards.summary: Track intake, weight trajectory, and BMI from diagnosis. An abnormal screen warrants assessment of symptoms, muscle, function, and inflammation. Normal BMI does not exclude clinically important nutritional deterioration.

cards.description: General adult energy and protein targets and their limitations
cards.summary: When individualized measurement is unavailable, estimate 25-30 kcal/kg/day. Protein should exceed 1 g/kg/day and, when feasible, approach 1.5 g/kg/day. These are adjustable estimates, not initial refeeding rates.

cards.description: Inadequate oral intake, dysphagia, mucositis, and a functioning gut
cards.summary: Escalate from counseling and oral supplements to enteral support when intake remains inadequate. PN becomes relevant when enteral support is infeasible or insufficient. Treat symptoms and assess swallowing safety.

cards.description: Intestinal failure, obstruction, PN burdens, prognosis, and goals
cards.locator: ESMO nutrition-support sections; ASCO nutritional recommendation 1.2
cards.summary: Intestinal failure can justify considering PN in selected patients; cachexia alone does not justify routine PN. Assess reversible causes, performance, anticipated benefit, prognosis, goals, and burdens. Comfort and symptom relief take priority near death; PN decisions require specialist discussion.

cards.description: Multifactorial wasting, counseling, and updated appetite-drug evidence
cards.locator: ASCO 2020 recommendations 1.1-1.2; ASCO 2023 recommendations 2.1-2.2; ESMO assessment
cards.summary: Cachexia involves disease-related metabolic changes and muscle loss, not simply low intake. Offer individualized dietitian input, nutrient-dense food, symptom care, and realistic goals. Routine tubes or PN are not established treatments for advanced-cancer cachexia alone. ASCO's 2023 update permits selected clinician-supervised low-dose olanzapine for appetite/weight; the supporting populations were mainly lung/GI cancers.

cards.description: High-risk nutrition restart, thiamine, electrolytes, and monitoring
cards.summary: BMI below 16 or low baseline phosphate, potassium, or magnesium indicates high refeeding risk. Use expert-supervised cautious initiation; NICE suggests at most 10 kcal/kg/day initially, with 5 in extreme cases, then gradual increase. Give thiamine before and during early feeding, replace electrolytes as needed, and monitor fluids, glucose, phosphate, magnesium, and potassium. Do not start full maintenance targets immediately. Rate and correction decisions require local clinical protocols.

cards.description: Neutropenia, unnecessary dietary restriction, and food hygiene
cards.locator: ASCO 2022 dietary recommendations; NCI reducing foodborne illness
cards.summary: A routinely restrictive neutropenic diet has not shown infection-prevention benefit and is not recommended by ASCO for that purpose. Emphasize hygiene, safe storage and cooking, and avoidance of unsafe raw/undercooked or unpasteurized products. Follow specific transplant-center protocols where applicable while protecting nutritional intake.

cards.description: High-dose vitamins/antioxidants, deficiency correction, and interactions
cards.summary: Use ordinary micronutrient intake rather than high doses without a demonstrated deficiency. Antioxidant supplements can interact with treatment, and safety/benefit evidence is uncertain. Review the exact products with the oncology team; food-based nutrition and clinician-directed deficiency correction are distinct from megadose supplementation.

cards.description: Pancreatic cancer, malabsorption, steatorrhea, and enzyme replacement
cards.summary: NICE recommends enteric-coated pancreatin for unresectable pancreatic cancer. Weight loss with greasy stools should prompt assessment of maldigestion and other causes, not only calorie advice. Enzyme selection, meal-time use, titration, and nutritional follow-up require the treating team; the source recommendation does not specify a universal dose.

cards.description: Fasting or ketogenic diets during treatment in a person losing weight
cards.locator: ESPEN recommendation 8; ASCO 2022 dietary evidence review
cards.summary: Avoid energy-restrictive diets in malnourished or at-risk patients. Evidence does not establish fasting or ketogenic diets as routine cancer-treatment adjuncts. Prioritize adequate intake and explain uncertainty without claiming diet cures cancer.

sources.title: [Obesity and cancer].
sources.authors: J-L Schlienger, F Luca, S Vinzio, A Pradignac
sources.abstract: Obesity which is now well recognized as a public health problem increases the risk of developing cancers. Some systematic review and meta-analyses assessed the strength of associations between body mass index and common cancers such as breast, endometrial, colon and adenocarcinoma of oesophagus. The causal mechanisms remain unexplained. However, epidemiological data and animal models have provided some evidence that hormonal alteration linked to obesity, such as hyperinsulinism, high insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1) levels or biodisponibility, low adiponectin serum level and high oestradiol serum level resulting from an enhanced aromatase activity may have mitogenic and antiapoptotic effects. The inflammation associated with visceral adiposity is another factor which promotes cancer. To date, there are no convincing data that weight loss could improve the prognosis of treated neoplasia. However, a regular physical activity and a limited caloric intake are probably safe in healthy subject to prevent cancer and also in cancer survivors.

sources.title: Cancer Cachexia: Identification by Clinical Assessment versus International Consensus Criteria in Patients with Metastatic Colorectal Cancer.
sources.authors: Anne van der Werf, Querijn N E van Bokhorst, Marian A E de van der Schueren, Henk M W Verheul, Jacqueline A E Langius
author_list: Marian A E de van der Schueren
sources.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cancer cachexia is associated with poorer outcomes and is often diagnosed by the Fearon criteria. Oncologists clinically identify cachexia based on a patient's presentation. In this study agreement between these identification methods was evaluated and associations with outcomes were studied in patients with metastatic colorectal cancer.
METHODS: Fearon criteria comprised weight loss >5% OR weight loss >2% with either BMI <20 kg/m2 or sarcopenia (determined by CT-imaging). Clinical assessment by the oncologist was based on the patient's clinical presentation. Agreement was tested with Kappa. Associations with treatment tolerance and progression free survival (PFS) were tested with logistic regressions and Cox proportional hazards, respectively.
RESULTS: Of 69 patients, 52% was identified as cachectic according to Fearon criteria and 9% according to clinical assessment. Agreement between both methods was slight (Kappa 0.049, P = 0.457). Clinically cachectic patients had a shorter PFS than clinically non-cachectic patients (HR 3.310, P = 0.016). No other differences in outcomes were found between cachectic vs. non-cachectic patients using both methods.
CONCLUSIONS: The agreement between cancer cachexia identification by clinical assessment vs. Fearon criteria was slight. Further improvement of cachexia criteria is necessary to identify cachectic patients at risk of poorer outcomes, who may benefit from targeted cachexia interventions.

sources.title: Nutritional prevention of colorectal cancer.
sources.authors: Mark A Hull
sources.journal: The Proceedings of the Nutrition Society
sources.abstract: The preventability estimate for colorectal cancer (CRC) is approximately 50%, highlighting the huge potential for altering modifiable lifestyle factors (including diet and body fatness) in order to reduce risk of this common malignancy. There is strong evidence that dietary factors (including intake of wholegrains, fibre, red and processed meat and alcohol) affect CRC risk. The lack of positive intervention trials and limited mechanistic understanding likely explain limited public health impact of epidemiological observations, to date. An alternative strategy for nutritional prevention of CRC is use of supplements that provide higher individual nutrient exposure than obtained through the diet (chemoprevention). There are positive data for calcium and/or vitamin D and the n-3 fatty acid EPA from polyp prevention trials using colorectal adenoma as a CRC risk biomarker. Although CRC is an obesity-related malignancy, there remains a paucity of observational data supporting intentional weight loss for CRC risk reduction. Some types of obesity surgeries (Roux-en-Y gastric bypass) might actually increase subsequent CRC risk due to alteration of local intestinal factors. There is intense interest in nutritional therapy of patients after diagnosis of CRC, in order to impact on recurrence and overall survival (now often termed cancer interception). In conclusion, nutritional prevention of CRC continues to hold much promise. Increased mechanistic understanding of the role of individual nutrients (linked to intestinal microbiota), as well as a precision medicine approach to CRC chemoprevention and interception based on both tumour and host factors, should enable translation of nutritional interventions into effective CRC risk reduction measures.

sources.title: Impact of oral nutritional supplements in post-discharge patients at nutritional risk following colorectal cancer surgery: A randomised clinical trial.
sources.authors: Shanjun Tan, Qingyang Meng, Yi Jiang, Qiulin Zhuang, Qiulei Xi, Jiahao Xu, Jinou Zhao, Xiangyu Sui, Guohao Wu
sources.abstract:
BACKGROUND & AIMS: Guidelines on clinical nutrition recommend the use of appropriate nutritional support therapy for surgical cancer patients at risk of malnutrition both during hospital care and following discharge from the hospital. However, previous studies regarding nutritional interventions have mainly focused on patients during their hospital stay; there is limited evidence supporting the recommendation of nutritional interventions for post-discharge patients after cancer surgery, particularly those who underwent gastrointestinal cancer surgery and at high risk of malnutrition. To clearly address this issue, we designed and conducted two independent studies on two different groups of post-discharge patients at nutritional risk after gastrointestinal cancer surgery. The present study aimed to assess the impact of oral nutritional supplements (ONS) in post-discharge patients at nutritional risk following colorectal cancer surgery. Meanwhile, the sister study on the use of ONS in post-discharge patients following gastric cancer surgery will be reported separately.
METHODS: Between January 2017 and June 2019, post-discharge patients following colorectal cancer surgery in our institution were randomised to receive either dietary advice alone (control group) or dietary advice in combination with ONS (ONS group) for three months if they were at nutritional risk based on the tool of Nutritional Risk Screening 2002. The primary endpoints were nutritional outcomes and sarcopenia prevalence. The secondary endpoints were 90-day readmission rate, chemotherapy tolerance, and quality of life (QoL).
RESULTS: Of the 232 eligible patients, 212 (107 in the control group and 105 in the ONS group) completed the trial. Their data were then analyzed. The mean ONS intake was 410 mL every day. By the three-month intervention, the skeletal muscle index in the ONS group was significantly higher than that in the control group (39.75 ± 5.83 vs 38.01 ± 6.18 cm2/m2, P = 0.037), but no significant differences between the two groups were noted in weight, weight loss, body mass index, serum albumin and hemoglobin (P > 0.05). In addition, the ONS group had a significantly lower sarcopenia prevalence (28.6% vs 42.1%, P = 0.040). No significant difference between the two groups was found in the 90-day readmission rate (P > 0.05). The number of patients undergoing postoperative chemotherapy in the two groups was similar, but chemotherapy modifications, such as delay, dose reduction, or termination, were significantly reduced in the ONS group (21.2% vs 36.8%, P=0.024). However, ONS had no significant effect on QoL (P > 0.05).
CONCLUSIONS: In post-discharge patients at nutritional risk following colorectal cancer surgery, the use of ONS may reduce skeletal muscle loss and sarcopenia prevalence, as well as improve chemotherapy tolerance, compared with dietary advice alone. These findings underline the importance of ONS treatment in post-discharge patients at nutritional risk following colorectal cancer surgery.

sources.title: Nutritional status and body composition assessment in patients with a new diagnosis of advanced solid tumour: Exploratory comparison of computed tomography and bioelectrical impedance analysis.
sources.authors: A Casirati, G Vandoni, S Della Valle, G Greco, M Platania, S Colatruglio, L Lalli, C Gavazzi
sources.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Low skeletal muscle is a common characteristic of cancer-related malnutrition and a predictor of poorer prognosis in oncological patients. In this study we evaluated nutritional status and altered body composition using computed tomography (CT) and bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) in newly diagnosed patients. Our purpose was to compare the results of two available techniques to assess body composition suggested by the guidelines and some diagnostic criteria to identify malnutrition.
METHODS: In a prospective study, patients with a new diagnosis of advanced solid tumour were enrolled and evaluated before starting first-line chemotherapy. Anthropometric, body composition and systemic inflammation measurements were collected and cut-off points from literature data were used for results classification. Malnutrition was expressed as weight loss (WL) in the previous 6 months >10% and underweight body mass index (BMI). Altered body composition was assessed as low index both skeletal muscle (SMI) derived by CT and fat-free mass by BIA (FFMI). Descriptive statistic was presented. Several statistical correlation analyses were performed.
RESULTS: 67 patients were assessed: 40M/27F; average age 59 ± 13 years and BMI 23 ± 4; 43 (64%) upper gastrointestinal, 12 lung, 9 colorectal, 3 other cancers. Fourty-five (67%) were malnourished with WL criteria but only 8 (12%) resulted underweight. From analysis of CT images and BIA, 49 (73%) and 10 (15%) patients respectively reported lower cut-off point. Overall, 35 (52%) had both sarcopenia and WL > 10%.
CONCLUSIONS: Our results suggest that prevalence data of malnutrition expressed as WL are more in agreement with those of sarcopenia recognised using CT than BIA method. Further studies are required to confirm these findings and to identify the best and easiest methods for monitoring BC during nutritional intervention and oncological therapies.

sources.title: The Spectrum of Malnutrition/Cachexia/Sarcopenia in Oncology According to Different Cancer Types and Settings: A Narrative Review.
sources.authors: Paolo Bossi, Paolo Delrio, Annalisa Mascheroni, Michela Zanetti
sources.abstract: Nutritional status in oncological patients may differ according to several modifiable and non-modifiable factors. Knowledge of the epidemiology of malnutrition/cachexia/sarcopenia may help to manage these complications early in the course of treatment, potentially impacting patient quality of life, treatment intensity, and disease outcome. Therefore, this narrative review aimed to critically evaluate the current evidence on the combined impact of tumor- and treatment-related factors on nutritional status and to draw some practical conclusions to support the multidisciplinary management of malnutrition in cancer patients. A comprehensive literature search was performed from January 2010 to December 2020 using different combinations of pertinent keywords and a critical evaluation of retrieved literature papers was conducted. The results show that the prevalence of weight loss and associated symptoms is quite heterogeneous and needs to be assessed with recognized criteria, thus allowing a clear classification and standardization of therapeutic interventions. There is a large range of variability influenced by age and social factors, comorbidities, and setting of cures (community-dwelling versus hospitalized patients). Tumor subsite is one of the major determinants of malnutrition, with pancreatic, esophageal, and other gastroenteric cancers, head and neck, and lung cancers having the highest prevalence. The advanced stage is also linked to a higher risk of developing malnutrition, as an expression of the relationship between tumor burden, inflammatory status, reduced caloric intake, and malabsorption. Finally, treatment type influences the risk of nutritional issues, both for locoregional approaches (surgery and radiotherapy) and for systemic treatment. Interestingly, personalized approaches based on the selection of the most predictive malnutrition definitions for postoperative complications according to cancer type and knowledge of specific nutritional problems associated with some new agents may positively impact disease course. Sharing common knowledge between oncologists and nutritionists may help to better address and treat malnutrition in this population.

sources.title: Prognostic value of systemic inflammation and for patients with colorectal cancer cachexia.
sources.authors: Guo-Tian Ruan, Hai-Lun Xie, Kai-Tao Yuan, Shi-Qi Lin, He-Yang Zhang, Chen-An Liu, Jin-Yu Shi, Yi-Zhong Ge, Meng-Meng Song, Chun-Lei Hu, Xiao-Wei Zhang, Xiao-Yue Liu, Ming Yang, Kun-Hua Wang, Xin Zheng, Yue Chen, Wen Hu, Ming-Hua Cong, Li-Chen Zhu, Li Deng, Han-Ping Shi
sources.journal: Journal of cachexia, sarcopenia and muscle
sources.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The development and progression of cancer cachexia are connected to systemic inflammation and physical performance. However, few relevant studies have reported the survival outcomes prediction of systemic inflammation and physical performance in patients with colorectal cancer (CRC) cachexia. This study investigated the prognostic prediction value of systemic inflammation and performance status in patients with CRC cachexia.
METHODS: This multicentre cohort study prospectively collected 905 patients with CRC (58.3% males, 59.3 ± 11.5 years old). Cancer cachexia was diagnosed according to the 2011 Fearon Cachexia Diagnostic Consensus. The prognostic value of systematic inflammatory indicators was determined using the area under the curve, concordance index, and multivariate survival analysis. Performance status was evaluated with Eastern Coopertive Oncology Group performance score (ECOG-PS). Survival data were analysed using univariate and multivariate Cox regression analyses.
RESULTS: The area under the curve, concordance index and survival analysis showed that C-reactive protein (CRP), lymphocyte to CRP ratio (LCR) and CRP to albumin ratio (CAR) were more stable and consistent with the survival of patients with CRC, both in non-cachexia and cachexia populations. Among patients with CRC cachexia, high inflammation [low LCR, hazard ratio (HR) 95% confidence interval (95% CI) = 3.33 (2.08-5.32); high CAR, HR (95% CI) = 2.92 (1.88-4.55); high CRP, HR (95% CI) = 3.12 (2.08-4.67)] indicated a worse prognosis, compared with non-cachexia patients [low LCR, HR (95% CI) = 2.28 (1.65-3.16); high CAR, HR (95% CI) = 2.36 (1.71-3.25); high CRP, HR (95% CI) = 2.58 (1.85-3.60)]. Similarly, among patients with CRC cachexia, high PS [ECOG-PS 2, HR (95% CI) = 1.61 (1.04-2.50); ECOG-PS 3/4, HR (95% CI) = 2.91 (1.69-5.00]) indicated a worse prognosis, compared with patients with CRC without cachexia [ECOG-PS 2, HR (95% CI) = 1.28 (0.90-1.81); ECOG-PS 3/4, HR (95% CI) = 2.41 (1.32-4.39]). Patients with CRC cachexia with an ECOG-PS score of 2 or 3-4 and a high inflammation had a shorter median survival time, compared with patients with an ECOG-PS score of 0/1 and a low inflammation.
CONCLUSIONS: The systemic inflammatory markers LCR, CAR and CRP have stable prognostic values in patients with CRC. The ECOG-PS may be an independent risk factor for CRC. Combined evaluation of systemic inflammation and ECOG-PS in patients with CRC cachexia could provide a simple survival prediction.

drafts:
**Direct answer:** No. A BMI of 25 does not exclude a clinically important nutritional problem. An 8 % unintentional weight loss over two months, combined with reduced intake in a patient starting colorectal-cancer (CRC) chemotherapy, constitutes a positive nutrition screen that warrants formal assessment and a dietitian referral regardless of the BMI category.

**Why BMI 25 is not reassuring**

Guidance is explicit that "normal BMI does not exclude clinically important nutritional deterioration" [S01]. The mechanism is straightforward: BMI conflates fat and lean mass. A patient who begins at a higher weight, or who loses skeletal muscle while retaining fat, can drift through the "overweight" BMI band while accumulating sarcopenia and cachexia. In a cohort of newly diagnosed advanced solid-tumour patients (mean BMI 23 ± 4), 67 % met malnutrition criteria by weight loss, yet only 12 % were underweight by BMI; 73 % had low CT-derived skeletal muscle index [P32873437]. The same study noted 52 % had both sarcopenia and >10 % weight loss, underscoring that BMI alone misses the majority of affected patients.

The 8 % loss also exceeds the >5 % threshold in the Fearon cachexia consensus (weight loss >5 %, or >2 % with BMI <20 or sarcopenia) used to flag cancer-related wasting [P30235002]. In that metastatic-CRC cohort, agreement between oncologists' clinical gestalt and formal criteria was only slight (Kappa 0.049), reinforcing the need for structured screening rather than impression [P30235002].

**Appropriate screening and follow-up**

- **Initial screen (diagnosis / pre-chemotherapy):** A validated tool such as NRS-2002, MUST, or PG-SGA, capturing unintentional weight loss, current oral intake, disease severity (cancer + active chemotherapy), and BMI. The NRS-2002 was the screening tool in the post-discharge CRC trial that showed benefit of oral nutritional supplements (ONS) in at-risk patients [P32563599] (note: that trial carries several published comments/corrections, so interpret its effect sizes cautiously).
- **Expanded assessment after a positive screen:** Symptom review (anorexia, nausea, mucositis, dysphagia, taste change), functional status (ECOG-PS), inflammatory markers (CRP, albumin, lymphocyte-to-CRP ratio), and, where available, body-composition imaging. In CRC cachexia, CRP, lymphocyte-to-CRP ratio, and CRP-to-albumin ratio, combined with ECOG-PS, independently predict survival [P37902006].
- **Cadence during treatment:** Re-weigh at each cycle (same scale, similar time of day), log 3-day dietary intake, reassess symptoms, and repeat screening if intake remains <60–70 % of estimated requirement. Track weight trajectory over 4–6 weeks; further >5 % loss or functional decline should trigger escalation.

**Practical intervention steps**

- Dietitian-led, individualized plan emphasising nutrient-dense, protein-rich food (target protein >1 g/kg/day, approaching 1.5 g/kg/day if tolerated; energy ≈ 25–30 kcal/kg/day as a starting estimate, not a rigid target) [S01].
- Oral nutritional supplements if intake stays inadequate; escalate to enteral support only if the gut is functional but oral intake remains insufficient [S01].
- Avoid energy-restrictive, fasting, or ketogenic "anti-cancer" diets in a patient already losing weight [S01][S05].
- This patient's BMI of 25 does **not** place them in a high-refeeding-risk category (NICE defines high risk as BMI <16 or low baseline phosphate/potassium/magnesium) [S04]; standard nutrition initiation is appropriate, with routine electrolyte monitoring rather than the ≤10 kcal/kg cautious protocol.
- Review any supplements or antioxidant products with the oncology team before use, given uncertain safety during chemotherapy [S06].

**Uncertainty and limits**

The actual body weight in kilograms, estimated current intake, specific chemo regimen and side-effect profile, and baseline labs are not provided, so precise kcal or protein numbers cannot be calculated here. The retrieved PubMed abstracts do not constitute full-text evidence; the P32563599 trial has multiple post-publication comments that may qualify its findings. The 2018 Fearon-criteria study [P30235002] involved only 69 metastatic-CRC patients, limiting generalisability to early-stage or curative-intent chemotherapy. Expert assessment by an oncology dietitian or clinical-nutrition team is the appropriate next step; the targets above are estimates, not a personalised prescription.

That study involved metastatic disease; the present patient's stage is unspecified, so the criterion serves as a screening flag rather than a confirmed cachexia diagnosis.

**Appropriate screening and assessment**

Guidance recommends tracking intake, weight trajectory, and BMI from diagnosis; an abnormal screen triggers assessment of symptoms, muscle, function, and inflammation [S01]. Commonly used oncology nutrition screens include NRS-2002, MUST, and PG-SGA, which capture unintentional weight loss, current intake, and disease severity. NRS-2002, for example, was used as a case-finding threshold in a post-surgical CRC population trial [P32563599]; that trial's purpose was to compare oral nutritional supplements (ONS) with dietary advice, not to validate the screening tool itself, and its population (post-discharge surgical patients) differs from a patient just starting systemic therapy. In that trial, ONS improved skeletal-muscle index (P = 0.037), lowered sarcopenia prevalence (28.6 % vs 42.1 %, P = 0.040), and reduced chemotherapy modifications (21.2 % vs 36.8 %, P = 0.024), but did not significantly change weight, BMI, albumin, or quality of life; four post-publication comments qualify the findings [P32563599].

After a positive screen, an expanded assessment should include symptom review (anorexia, nausea, mucositis, dysphagia), functional status (ECOG-PS), inflammatory markers (CRP, albumin, lymphocyte-to-CRP ratio), and, where feasible, body-composition imaging. In CRC, high CRP, CRP-to-albumin ratio, low lymphocyte-to-CRP ratio, and ECOG-PS ≥ 2 independently predicted worse survival in cachectic patients [P37902006].

**Follow-up cadence and intervention**

The guidance principle is to "track intake, weight trajectory, and BMI" across the treatment course [S01]. Specific cadence—re-weighing each cycle, a 3-day dietary recall, and re-screening when intake falls below roughly 60–70 % of estimated requirement—is reasonable expert practice rather than a guideline-mandated threshold. Escalate from dietary counselling and ONS to enteral support if oral intake remains inadequate with a functioning gut [S01][S08]. Energy ≈ 25–30 kcal/kg/day and protein > 1 g/kg/day (toward 1.5 g/kg/day if tolerated) are adjustable starting estimates, not rigid targets or refeeding rates [S01]. This patient's BMI of 25 does not place them in a high-refeeding-risk category (NICE: BMI < 16 or low baseline phosphate/potassium/magnesium), so a ≤ 10 kcal/kg cautious protocol is not indicated [S04]. Avoid energy-restrictive or ketogenic "anti-cancer" diets while the patient is losing weight [S01][S05]. Review any supplement or antioxidant product with the oncology team before use [S06].

**Uncertainty and limits**

Actual body weight in kilograms, estimated current intake, specific regimen and side-effect profile, baseline electrolytes, and ECOG-PS are unavailable, so precise caloric or protein figures cannot be calculated. The PubMed abstracts retrieved here are title/abstract-level evidence; full-text methods, subgroup data, and the post-publication comments on [P32563599] may alter interpretation. Expert assessment by an oncology dietitian or clinical-nutrition team is the appropriate next step; the estimates above are planning ranges, not a personalised prescription.

issues: P32563599 is cited to support the use of NRS-2002 as an appropriate screening tool, but the paper's purpose is to evaluate ONS intervention in post-discharge CRC surgery patients; NRS-2002 was merely an inclusion criterion, not the subject of validation. The citation does not demonstrate that NRS-2002 is a preferred or validated screening tool over MUST or PG-SGA.

Follow-up parameters (re-weigh each cycle, 3-day dietary log, re-screen at <60–70 % of estimated requirement) are presented in a structured protocol format without source attribution. The supplied guidance (G01) states 'track intake, weight trajectory, and BMI' but does not specify cadence, log duration, or a percentage threshold. These are reasonable clinical suggestions but should be flagged as expert-practice recommendations, not guideline-mandated steps.

The P32563599 finding is described as showing 'benefit of ONS in at-risk patients.' answer:
**Direct answer.** No—a BMI of 25 does not exclude a clinically important nutritional problem. In a patient starting colorectal-cancer (CRC) chemotherapy with 8 % unintentional weight loss over two months and reduced intake, the screen is positive and warrants formal assessment and dietitian referral irrespective of BMI category [S01].

**Why BMI 25 is not reassuring**

BMI conflates fat and lean mass. A patient losing skeletal muscle while retaining adipose tissue can remain in the "overweight" band while developing sarcopenia and early cachexia [S01]. In 67 newly diagnosed advanced solid-tumour patients (mean BMI 23 ± 4; 9 with CRC), 67 % met malnutrition criteria by weight loss yet only 12 % were underweight by BMI; 73 % had a below-cut-off CT skeletal-muscle index [P32873437]. The 8 % loss also crosses the >5 % weight-loss threshold in the Fearon cachexia consensus as applied in a 69-patient metastatic-CRC cohort, where structured criteria identified 52 % as cachectic versus 9 % by clinician impression alone (Kappa 0.049) [P30235002]. That study involved metastatic disease; the present patient's stage is unspecified, so the criterion serves as a screening flag rather than a confirmed cachexia diagnosis.

**Appropriate screening and assessment**

Guidance recommends tracking intake, weight trajectory, and BMI from diagnosis; an abnormal screen triggers assessment of symptoms, muscle, function, and inflammation [S01]. Commonly used oncology nutrition screens include NRS-2002, MUST, and PG-SGA, which capture unintentional weight loss, current intake, and disease severity. NRS-2002, for example, was used as a case-finding threshold in a post-surgical CRC population trial [P32563599]; that trial's purpose was to compare oral nutritional supplements (ONS) with dietary advice, not to validate the screening tool itself, and its population (post-discharge surgical patients) differs from a patient just starting systemic therapy. In that trial, ONS improved skeletal-muscle index (P = 0.037), lowered sarcopenia prevalence (28.6 % vs 42.1 %, P = 0.040), and reduced chemotherapy modifications (21.2 % vs 36.8 %, P = 0.024), but did not significantly change weight, BMI, albumin, or quality of life; four post-publication comments qualify the findings [P32563599].

After a positive screen, an expanded assessment should include symptom review (anorexia, nausea, mucositis, dysphagia), functional status (ECOG-PS), inflammatory markers (CRP, albumin, lymphocyte-to-CRP ratio), and, where feasible, body-composition imaging. In CRC, high CRP, CRP-to-albumin ratio, low lymphocyte-to-CRP ratio, and ECOG-PS ≥ 2 independently predicted worse survival in cachectic patients [P37902006].

**Follow-up cadence and intervention**

The guidance principle is to "track intake, weight trajectory, and BMI" across the treatment course [S01]. Specific cadence—re-weighing each cycle, a 3-day dietary recall, and re-screening when intake falls below roughly 60–70 % of estimated requirement—is reasonable expert practice rather than a guideline-mandated threshold. Escalate from dietary counselling and ONS to enteral support if oral intake remains inadequate with a functioning gut [S01][S08]. Energy ≈ 25–30 kcal/kg/day and protein > 1 g/kg/day (toward 1.5 g/kg/day if tolerated) are adjustable starting estimates, not rigid targets or refeeding rates [S01]. This patient's BMI of 25 does not place them in a high-refeeding-risk category (NICE: BMI < 16 or low baseline phosphate/potassium/magnesium), so a ≤ 10 kcal/kg cautious protocol is not indicated [S04]. Avoid energy-restrictive or ketogenic "anti-cancer" diets while the patient is losing weight [S01][S05]. Review any supplement or antioxidant product with the oncology team before use [S06].

**Uncertainty and limits**

Actual body weight in kilograms, estimated current intake, specific regimen and side-effect profile, baseline electrolytes, and ECOG-PS are unavailable, so precise caloric or protein figures cannot be calculated. The PubMed abstracts retrieved here are title/abstract-level evidence; full-text methods, subgroup data, and the post-publication comments on [P32563599] may alter interpretation. Expert assessment by an oncology dietitian or clinical-nutrition team is the appropriate next step; the estimates above are planning ranges, not a personalised prescription.

sources.title: Cancer Cachexia: Identification by Clinical Assessment versus International Consensus Criteria in Patients with Metastatic Colorectal Cancer.
sources.authors: Anne van der Werf, Querijn N E van Bokhorst, Marian A E de van der Schueren, Henk M W Verheul, Jacqueline A E Langius
author_list: Marian A E de van der Schueren
sources.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cancer cachexia is associated with poorer outcomes and is often diagnosed by the Fearon criteria. Oncologists clinically identify cachexia based on a patient's presentation. In this study agreement between these identification methods was evaluated and associations with outcomes were studied in patients with metastatic colorectal cancer.
METHODS: Fearon criteria comprised weight loss >5% OR weight loss >2% with either BMI <20 kg/m2 or sarcopenia (determined by CT-imaging). Clinical assessment by the oncologist was based on the patient's clinical presentation. Agreement was tested with Kappa. Associations with treatment tolerance and progression free survival (PFS) were tested with logistic regressions and Cox proportional hazards, respectively.
RESULTS: Of 69 patients, 52% was identified as cachectic according to Fearon criteria and 9% according to clinical assessment. Agreement between both methods was slight (Kappa 0.049, P = 0.457). Clinically cachectic patients had a shorter PFS than clinically non-cachectic patients (HR 3.310, P = 0.016). No other differences in outcomes were found between cachectic vs. non-cachectic patients using both methods.
CONCLUSIONS: The agreement between cancer cachexia identification by clinical assessment vs. Fearon criteria was slight. Further improvement of cachexia criteria is necessary to identify cachectic patients at risk of poorer outcomes, who may benefit from targeted cachexia interventions.

sources.title: Impact of oral nutritional supplements in post-discharge patients at nutritional risk following colorectal cancer surgery: A randomised clinical trial.
sources.authors: Shanjun Tan, Qingyang Meng, Yi Jiang, Qiulin Zhuang, Qiulei Xi, Jiahao Xu, Jinou Zhao, Xiangyu Sui, Guohao Wu
sources.abstract:
BACKGROUND & AIMS: Guidelines on clinical nutrition recommend the use of appropriate nutritional support therapy for surgical cancer patients at risk of malnutrition both during hospital care and following discharge from the hospital. However, previous studies regarding nutritional interventions have mainly focused on patients during their hospital stay; there is limited evidence supporting the recommendation of nutritional interventions for post-discharge patients after cancer surgery, particularly those who underwent gastrointestinal cancer surgery and at high risk of malnutrition. To clearly address this issue, we designed and conducted two independent studies on two different groups of post-discharge patients at nutritional risk after gastrointestinal cancer surgery. The present study aimed to assess the impact of oral nutritional supplements (ONS) in post-discharge patients at nutritional risk following colorectal cancer surgery. Meanwhile, the sister study on the use of ONS in post-discharge patients following gastric cancer surgery will be reported separately.
METHODS: Between January 2017 and June 2019, post-discharge patients following colorectal cancer surgery in our institution were randomised to receive either dietary advice alone (control group) or dietary advice in combination with ONS (ONS group) for three months if they were at nutritional risk based on the tool of Nutritional Risk Screening 2002. The primary endpoints were nutritional outcomes and sarcopenia prevalence. The secondary endpoints were 90-day readmission rate, chemotherapy tolerance, and quality of life (QoL).
RESULTS: Of the 232 eligible patients, 212 (107 in the control group and 105 in the ONS group) completed the trial. Their data were then analyzed. The mean ONS intake was 410 mL every day. By the three-month intervention, the skeletal muscle index in the ONS group was significantly higher than that in the control group (39.75 ± 5.83 vs 38.01 ± 6.18 cm2/m2, P = 0.037), but no significant differences between the two groups were noted in weight, weight loss, body mass index, serum albumin and hemoglobin (P > 0.05). In addition, the ONS group had a significantly lower sarcopenia prevalence (28.6% vs 42.1%, P = 0.040). No significant difference between the two groups was found in the 90-day readmission rate (P > 0.05). The number of patients undergoing postoperative chemotherapy in the two groups was similar, but chemotherapy modifications, such as delay, dose reduction, or termination, were significantly reduced in the ONS group (21.2% vs 36.8%, P=0.024). However, ONS had no significant effect on QoL (P > 0.05).
CONCLUSIONS: In post-discharge patients at nutritional risk following colorectal cancer surgery, the use of ONS may reduce skeletal muscle loss and sarcopenia prevalence, as well as improve chemotherapy tolerance, compared with dietary advice alone. These findings underline the importance of ONS treatment in post-discharge patients at nutritional risk following colorectal cancer surgery.

sources.title: Nutritional status and body composition assessment in patients with a new diagnosis of advanced solid tumour: Exploratory comparison of computed tomography and bioelectrical impedance analysis.
sources.authors: A Casirati, G Vandoni, S Della Valle, G Greco, M Platania, S Colatruglio, L Lalli, C Gavazzi
sources.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Low skeletal muscle is a common characteristic of cancer-related malnutrition and a predictor of poorer prognosis in oncological patients. In this study we evaluated nutritional status and altered body composition using computed tomography (CT) and bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) in newly diagnosed patients. Our purpose was to compare the results of two available techniques to assess body composition suggested by the guidelines and some diagnostic criteria to identify malnutrition.
METHODS: In a prospective study, patients with a new diagnosis of advanced solid tumour were enrolled and evaluated before starting first-line chemotherapy. Anthropometric, body composition and systemic inflammation measurements were collected and cut-off points from literature data were used for results classification. Malnutrition was expressed as weight loss (WL) in the previous 6 months >10% and underweight body mass index (BMI). Altered body composition was assessed as low index both skeletal muscle (SMI) derived by CT and fat-free mass by BIA (FFMI). Descriptive statistic was presented. Several statistical correlation analyses were performed.
RESULTS: 67 patients were assessed: 40M/27F; average age 59 ± 13 years and BMI 23 ± 4; 43 (64%) upper gastrointestinal, 12 lung, 9 colorectal, 3 other cancers. Fourty-five (67%) were malnourished with WL criteria but only 8 (12%) resulted underweight. From analysis of CT images and BIA, 49 (73%) and 10 (15%) patients respectively reported lower cut-off point. Overall, 35 (52%) had both sarcopenia and WL > 10%.
CONCLUSIONS: Our results suggest that prevalence data of malnutrition expressed as WL are more in agreement with those of sarcopenia recognised using CT than BIA method. Further studies are required to confirm these findings and to identify the best and easiest methods for monitoring BC during nutritional intervention and oncological therapies.

sources.title: Prognostic value of systemic inflammation and for patients with colorectal cancer cachexia.
sources.authors: Guo-Tian Ruan, Hai-Lun Xie, Kai-Tao Yuan, Shi-Qi Lin, He-Yang Zhang, Chen-An Liu, Jin-Yu Shi, Yi-Zhong Ge, Meng-Meng Song, Chun-Lei Hu, Xiao-Wei Zhang, Xiao-Yue Liu, Ming Yang, Kun-Hua Wang, Xin Zheng, Yue Chen, Wen Hu, Ming-Hua Cong, Li-Chen Zhu, Li Deng, Han-Ping Shi
sources.journal: Journal of cachexia, sarcopenia and muscle
sources.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The development and progression of cancer cachexia are connected to systemic inflammation and physical performance. However, few relevant studies have reported the survival outcomes prediction of systemic inflammation and physical performance in patients with colorectal cancer (CRC) cachexia. This study investigated the prognostic prediction value of systemic inflammation and performance status in patients with CRC cachexia.
METHODS: This multicentre cohort study prospectively collected 905 patients with CRC (58.3% males, 59.3 ± 11.5 years old). Cancer cachexia was diagnosed according to the 2011 Fearon Cachexia Diagnostic Consensus. The prognostic value of systematic inflammatory indicators was determined using the area under the curve, concordance index, and multivariate survival analysis. Performance status was evaluated with Eastern Coopertive Oncology Group performance score (ECOG-PS). Survival data were analysed using univariate and multivariate Cox regression analyses.
RESULTS: The area under the curve, concordance index and survival analysis showed that C-reactive protein (CRP), lymphocyte to CRP ratio (LCR) and CRP to albumin ratio (CAR) were more stable and consistent with the survival of patients with CRC, both in non-cachexia and cachexia populations. Among patients with CRC cachexia, high inflammation [low LCR, hazard ratio (HR) 95% confidence interval (95% CI) = 3.33 (2.08-5.32); high CAR, HR (95% CI) = 2.92 (1.88-4.55); high CRP, HR (95% CI) = 3.12 (2.08-4.67)] indicated a worse prognosis, compared with non-cachexia patients [low LCR, HR (95% CI) = 2.28 (1.65-3.16); high CAR, HR (95% CI) = 2.36 (1.71-3.25); high CRP, HR (95% CI) = 2.58 (1.85-3.60)]. Similarly, among patients with CRC cachexia, high PS [ECOG-PS 2, HR (95% CI) = 1.61 (1.04-2.50); ECOG-PS 3/4, HR (95% CI) = 2.91 (1.69-5.00]) indicated a worse prognosis, compared with patients with CRC without cachexia [ECOG-PS 2, HR (95% CI) = 1.28 (0.90-1.81); ECOG-PS 3/4, HR (95% CI) = 2.41 (1.32-4.39]). Patients with CRC cachexia with an ECOG-PS score of 2 or 3-4 and a high inflammation had a shorter median survival time, compared with patients with an ECOG-PS score of 0/1 and a low inflammation.
CONCLUSIONS: The systemic inflammatory markers LCR, CAR and CRP have stable prognostic values in patients with CRC. The ECOG-PS may be an independent risk factor for CRC. Combined evaluation of systemic inflammation and ECOG-PS in patients with CRC cachexia could provide a simple survival prediction.

**Direct answer:** No. A BMI of 25 does not exclude a clinically important nutritional problem. An 8 % unintentional weight loss over two months, combined with reduced intake in a patient starting colorectal-cancer (CRC) chemotherapy, constitutes a positive nutrition screen that warrants formal assessment and a dietitian referral regardless of the BMI category.

**Why BMI 25 is not reassuring**

Guidance is explicit that "normal BMI does not exclude clinically important nutritional deterioration" [S01]. The mechanism is straightforward: BMI conflates fat and lean mass. A patient who begins at a higher weight, or who loses skeletal muscle while retaining fat, can drift through the "overweight" BMI band while accumulating sarcopenia and cachexia. In a cohort of newly diagnosed advanced solid-tumour patients (mean BMI 23 ± 4), 67 % met malnutrition criteria by weight loss, yet only 12 % were underweight by BMI; 73 % had low CT-derived skeletal muscle index [P32873437]. The same study noted 52 % had both sarcopenia and >10 % weight loss, underscoring that BMI alone misses the majority of affected patients.

The 8 % loss also exceeds the >5 % threshold in the Fearon cachexia consensus (weight loss >5 %, or >2 % with BMI <20 or sarcopenia) used to flag cancer-related wasting [P30235002]. In that metastatic-CRC cohort, agreement between oncologists' clinical gestalt and formal criteria was only slight (Kappa 0.049), reinforcing the need for structured screening rather than impression [P30235002].

**Appropriate screening and follow-up**

- **Initial screen (diagnosis / pre-chemotherapy):** A validated tool such as NRS-2002, MUST, or PG-SGA, capturing unintentional weight loss, current oral intake, disease severity (cancer + active chemotherapy), and BMI. The NRS-2002 was the screening tool in the post-discharge CRC trial that showed benefit of oral nutritional supplements (ONS) in at-risk patients [P32563599] (note: that trial carries several published comments/corrections, so interpret its effect sizes cautiously).
- **Expanded assessment after a positive screen:** Symptom review (anorexia, nausea, mucositis, dysphagia, taste change), functional status (ECOG-PS), inflammatory markers (CRP, albumin, lymphocyte-to-CRP ratio), and, where available, body-composition imaging. In CRC cachexia, CRP, lymphocyte-to-CRP ratio, and CRP-to-albumin ratio, combined with ECOG-PS, independently predict survival [P37902006].
- **Cadence during treatment:** Re-weigh at each cycle (same scale, similar time of day), log 3-day dietary intake, reassess symptoms, and repeat screening if intake remains <60–70 % of estimated requirement. Track weight trajectory over 4–6 weeks; further >5 % loss or functional decline should trigger escalation.

**Practical intervention steps**

- Dietitian-led, individualized plan emphasising nutrient-dense, protein-rich food (target protein >1 g/kg/day, approaching 1.5 g/kg/day if tolerated; energy ≈ 25–30 kcal/kg/day as a starting estimate, not a rigid target) [S01].
- Oral nutritional supplements if intake stays inadequate; escalate to enteral support only if the gut is functional but oral intake remains insufficient [S01].
- Avoid energy-restrictive, fasting, or ketogenic "anti-cancer" diets in a patient already losing weight [S01][S05].
- This patient's BMI of 25 does **not** place them in a high-refeeding-risk category (NICE defines high risk as BMI <16 or low baseline phosphate/potassium/magnesium) [S04]; standard nutrition initiation is appropriate, with routine electrolyte monitoring rather than the ≤10 kcal/kg cautious protocol.
- Review any supplements or antioxidant products with the oncology team before use, given uncertain safety during chemotherapy [S06].

**Uncertainty and limits**

The actual body weight in kilograms, estimated current intake, specific chemo regimen and side-effect profile, and baseline labs are not provided, so precise kcal or protein numbers cannot be calculated here. The retrieved PubMed abstracts do not constitute full-text evidence; the P32563599 trial has multiple post-publication comments that may qualify its findings. The 2018 Fearon-criteria study [P30235002] involved only 69 metastatic-CRC patients, limiting generalisability to early-stage or curative-intent chemotherapy. Expert assessment by an oncology dietitian or clinical-nutrition team is the appropriate next step; the targets above are estimates, not a personalised prescription.

**Direct answer.** No—a BMI of 25 does not exclude a clinically important nutritional problem. In a patient starting colorectal-cancer (CRC) chemotherapy with 8 % unintentional weight loss over two months and reduced intake, the screen is positive and warrants formal assessment and dietitian referral irrespective of BMI category [S01].

**Why BMI 25 is not reassuring**

BMI conflates fat and lean mass. A patient losing skeletal muscle while retaining adipose tissue can remain in the "overweight" band while developing sarcopenia and early cachexia [S01]. In 67 newly diagnosed advanced solid-tumour patients (mean BMI 23 ± 4; 9 with CRC), 67 % met malnutrition criteria by weight loss yet only 12 % were underweight by BMI; 73 % had a below-cut-off CT skeletal-muscle index [P32873437]. The 8 % loss also crosses the >5 % weight-loss threshold in the Fearon cachexia consensus as applied in a 69-patient metastatic-CRC cohort, where structured criteria identified 52 % as cachectic versus 9 % by clinician impression alone (Kappa 0.049) [P30235002]. That study involved metastatic disease; the present patient's stage is unspecified, so the criterion serves as a screening flag rather than a confirmed cachexia diagnosis.

**Appropriate screening and assessment**

Guidance recommends tracking intake, weight trajectory, and BMI from diagnosis; an abnormal screen triggers assessment of symptoms, muscle, function, and inflammation [S01]. Commonly used oncology nutrition screens include NRS-2002, MUST, and PG-SGA, which capture unintentional weight loss, current intake, and disease severity. NRS-2002, for example, was used as a case-finding threshold in a post-surgical CRC population trial [P32563599]; that trial's purpose was to compare oral nutritional supplements (ONS) with dietary advice, not to validate the screening tool itself, and its population (post-discharge surgical patients) differs from a patient just starting systemic therapy. In that trial, ONS improved skeletal-muscle index (P = 0.037), lowered sarcopenia prevalence (28.6 % vs 42.1 %, P = 0.040), and reduced chemotherapy modifications (21.2 % vs 36.8 %, P = 0.024), but did not significantly change weight, BMI, albumin, or quality of life; four post-publication comments qualify the findings [P32563599].

After a positive screen, an expanded assessment should include symptom review (anorexia, nausea, mucositis, dysphagia), functional status (ECOG-PS), inflammatory markers (CRP, albumin, lymphocyte-to-CRP ratio), and, where feasible, body-composition imaging. In CRC, high CRP, CRP-to-albumin ratio, low lymphocyte-to-CRP ratio, and ECOG-PS ≥ 2 independently predicted worse survival in cachectic patients [P37902006].

**Follow-up cadence and intervention**

The guidance principle is to "track intake, weight trajectory, and BMI" across the treatment course [S01]. Specific cadence—re-weighing each cycle, a 3-day dietary recall, and re-screening when intake falls below roughly 60–70 % of estimated requirement—is reasonable expert practice rather than a guideline-mandated threshold. Escalate from dietary counselling and ONS to enteral support if oral intake remains inadequate with a functioning gut [S01][S08]. Energy ≈ 25–30 kcal/kg/day and protein > 1 g/kg/day (toward 1.5 g/kg/day if tolerated) are adjustable starting estimates, not rigid targets or refeeding rates [S01]. This patient's BMI of 25 does not place them in a high-refeeding-risk category (NICE: BMI < 16 or low baseline phosphate/potassium/magnesium), so a ≤ 10 kcal/kg cautious protocol is not indicated [S04]. Avoid energy-restrictive or ketogenic "anti-cancer" diets while the patient is losing weight [S01][S05]. Review any supplement or antioxidant product with the oncology team before use [S06].

**Uncertainty and limits**

Actual body weight in kilograms, estimated current intake, specific regimen and side-effect profile, baseline electrolytes, and ECOG-PS are unavailable, so precise caloric or protein figures cannot be calculated. The PubMed abstracts retrieved here are title/abstract-level evidence; full-text methods, subgroup data, and the post-publication comments on [P32563599] may alter interpretation. Expert assessment by an oncology dietitian or clinical-nutrition team is the appropriate next step; the estimates above are planning ranges, not a personalised prescription.
